Your website was finished two years ago.
The internet wasn't.

It gets visitors, but the phone isn't ringing. Traffic without leads is decoration.
Nobody owns it. Updates pile up, plugins age, and the one person who "knows the website" left last spring.

work.heroHeadline: Not a gallery. A track record.
work.heroLede: Pretty screenshots don't pay your invoices. These are the stories of what changed for the businesses behind the websites — including what happened a year after launch.

cases.situation: A respected two-partner firm whose reputation was built on referrals — and whose website looked like it. By the time a referred prospect finished "checking them out online," the polish of the in-person experience had already been undercut.
cases.problem: The site took six seconds to load, didn't work on phones, and was invisible for every search a potential client might actually type. It answered no questions and asked for nothing.
cases.approach: We rebuilt the firm's presence around the questions clients ask before hiring a lawyer — fees, process, outcomes — and gave every page one job: start a conversation. Local SEO put the firm on the map for the searches that matter.
cases.partnership: Eighteen months later, we still meet quarterly. Leads are up another 40% on year one, and the firm has added two associates to handle the volume.

cases.situation: Twelve trucks, twenty years in business, and a feast-or-famine lead flow that depended entirely on word of mouth and a fading spot in a paper directory.
cases.problem: Searching "furnace repair" in their own service area brought up three competitors before them. Their site had no way to book, no reviews, and no reason to call.
cases.approach: A conversion-first rebuild: click-to-call everywhere, service-area pages for every town they cover, review integration, and a Google Business Profile overhaul. Then a Care Plan, because an HVAC owner has no time to think about websites — that's the point.

cases.partnership: Two winters in, seasonal campaign pages go up every October without Ray ever asking. "The phone rings now. That's the whole review."

cases.situation: A restaurant whose dining room was unforgettable and whose website was a PDF menu from 2019. Nearly every reservation arrived through third-party platforms — along with their commissions.
cases.problem: The brand experience ended at the door. Online, Olive & Ash looked like every other restaurant, and paid a platform for the privilege.
cases.approach: A photography-led rebuild that put the room, the food, and the story first — with direct reservations one tap away on every page. Own your guests; don't rent them.
cases.partnership: Menus update the day they change. Seasonal campaigns land on schedule. Three years on, Maria has never logged into the CMS — and never needed to.

about.heroHeadline: Websites are projects to everyone else. To us, they're a responsibility.
about.whyHeadline: Too many good businesses are held back by bad websites.
about.whyLede: HAND started with a pattern we kept seeing: excellent businesses — skilled, trusted, busy — represented online by something that undersold everything they'd built. Not because they didn't care, but because nobody had ever taken real ownership of their presence.
about.whyPara2: The agency would launch and leave. The freelancer would drift away. The "website person" would change jobs. And the site would quietly decay while the business it represented kept getting better.
about.whyPara3: So we built the company we kept wishing existed: one partner, permanently accountable, for everything your business is online. Handcrafted work, hands-on care — your presence in good hands. That's the name, and that's the whole idea.

items.q: How much does a website cost?
items.a: Most HAND projects land between $10,000 and $50,000 depending on scope, with Care Plans from a few hundred dollars per month and growth retainers scaled to ambition. We publish ranges because "it depends — book a call" wastes your time. If your budget is under $10k, a template-based option may genuinely serve you better, and we'll tell you so on the discovery call.

items.q: Will I be locked in to you?
items.a: No — and this is in writing in every contract. You own everything: code, content, design files, domains, and accounts, all in your name from day one. If you ever leave, we'll help you migrate. Clients stay because they want to; 94% are still with us after year one.

Launch is day one, not goodbye. Every project moves into a Care Plan — hosting, security, backups, updates, and monthly content hours under a 24-hour response SLA. Most clients add quarterly growth reviews, where we look at the numbers and decide what to improve next.

items.q: How long does a project take?
items.a: Most sites launch in six to eight weeks from the strategy kickoff. You'll have the exact date before we start — and our launch-date guarantee means that if we miss it, you don't pay the final installment until we're done.

items.q: How much of my time will this take?
items.a: About three hours total before launch: a discovery call, a strategy session, three short design reviews, and a handover. We structured the process so you can delegate the outcome instead of managing the project.

items.q: We already have a website. Do we have to start over?
items.a: Not necessarily. The free audit will tell you honestly whether your current site is worth improving or genuinely holding you back. Sometimes the right answer is a focused round of fixes plus a Care Plan — and when it is, that's what we'll recommend.

items.q: What makes HAND different from other agencies?
items.a: The model. Most agencies are built around projects: pitch, build, launch, goodbye. HAND is built around partnership: the majority of our work is the ongoing care, optimization, and growth of sites we've launched. That changes the incentives — we build things we'll have to maintain, and our best marketing is your year-two results.

items.q: Do you work with businesses in any industry?
items.a: We focus where we're strongest: professional services, home services and trades, healthcare, hospitality, and B2B manufacturing. If you're outside those, the discovery call will sort out fit quickly — and if we're wrong for you, we'll point you toward someone better suited.
